strengths: Provides a theoretical justification (Theorem 1) for replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution in diffusion models with a conditionally whitened Gaussian, giving a sufficient condition (KL divergence reduction) that motivates the design choices rather than being purely heuristic.

Proposes a unified and general framework (CW-Gen) that subsumes prior mean/variance-regressor approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases and can be seamlessly integrated as a plug-in module into diverse existing diffusion and flow-matching backbones.

The Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) jointly models the conditional mean and sliding-window covariance with a Cholesky-based PSD parameterization and an eigenvalue regularization term, directly linked to the theoretical sufficient condition, which is a reasonably principled design.
Extends the whitening idea beyond diffusion (CW-Diff) to flow matching (CW-Flow), improving computational efficiency by avoiding explicit matrix inversion at each step.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: 5 datasets, 6 base generative models (both diffusion and flow-based), 4 main metrics plus 2 additional point-forecast metrics, 10 random seeds with standard deviations reported, and win-rate summaries showing fairly consistent improvement.
Qualitative illustrations (Figure 2) support the claim that CW-Gen mitigates distribution shift and produces tighter, more accurate uncertainty bands compared to non-whitened counterparts.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 gives only a sufficient (not necessary) condition and is stated as an inequality that is difficult to interpret in practice; there is no empirical verification that the condition actually holds for the trained JMCE estimators on the real datasets, weakening the claimed link between theory and observed empirical gains.

The comparison between CW-Gen and baseline prior-informed methods (TMDM, NsDiff) is somewhat unfair/confounded since CW-Gen uses a more powerful Non-stationary Transformer backbone for JMCE, whereas baselines use their original (often simpler) regressors; it's unclear how much of the gain is due to the whitening idea versus the stronger estimator architecture.

Win-rate reporting (e.g., 'CW-Gen outperforms in 22/24 cases') aggregates across metrics/models/datasets without statistical significance testing, and given the noticeable overlap in reported standard deviations (e.g., TMDM/NSDiff CRPS in Table 2), some improvements may not be statistically significant.

Only one dataset (ETTh1) is shown in the main text with full result tables; results for ETTh2, ILI, Weather, and Solar Energy are deferred to tables 3-6 not shown in the excerpt, making it hard to fully assess consistency of gains, especially on higher-dimensional data (Solar Energy has notably lower win rate at 79%).

The computational overhead of training JMCE (an additional non-autoregressive Transformer model) and its cost during inference is not clearly quantified or compared against baseline runtime/parameter counts, despite claiming CW-Flow's efficiency advantage over CW-Diff.

The paper doesn't sufficiently discuss failure cases or limitations of the method, e.g., when covariance estimation is poor or in very high-dimensional settings where O(d^3) eigendecomposition (for CW-Diff) could become a bottleneck.

The relationship and comparative advantage of CW-Gen over NsDiff (which also models heteroscedasticity via mean/variance regressors) is asserted qualitatively but not tightly established: Theorem 2 (comparing against TMDM/NsDiff) is relegated entirely to the appendix and not discussed in the main text, leaving the core novelty argument against the closest baseline under-supported in the main paper.

Notational density and heavy reliance on appendices (proofs, algorithms, extra results) makes the main paper harder to verify standalone; several key implementation details (e.g., choice of window size, architecture specifics of JMCE) are deferred, limiting reproducibility from the main text alone.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: incorporating conditional mean/covariance priors into diffusion and flow-matching models for probabilistic time series forecasting, unifying several prior works (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases of a more general whitening framework.

The idea of conditionally whitening the data (via joint mean and sliding-window covariance estimation) before training a diffusion/flow model is a reasonably clean and interpretable mechanism, and the paper extends the idea naturally to flow matching (CW-Flow), which is architecturally simpler and avoids matrix-inversion cost at inference.

Theorem 1 provides an interpretable, if loose, sufficient condition connecting estimator accuracy of the mean/covariance to a reduction in the KL divergence between the data distribution and the terminal (prior) distribution of a diffusion model, giving some theoretical grounding to the design of the JMCE loss.

The empirical study spans five datasets and integrates CW-Gen into six different backbone generative models, which is a reasonably broad evaluation protocol, and includes qualitative illustrations suggesting CW variants reduce mean-shift/distribution-shift artifacts.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea of replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution with a conditional Gaussian parameterized by learned mean/covariance is already present in CARD, TMDM, and especially NsDiff (mean + variance regressors); the paper's main technical addition is a joint Cholesky-based covariance estimator and a reformulation as a whitening transform, which is a fairly modest increment over existing prior-informed diffusion approaches, despite being framed as a fundamentally new paradigm.

Theorem 1 is only a sufficient (not necessary) condition and is quite loose in practice: it requires knowledge of unknown ground-truth ΣX|C to even evaluate the left/right-hand sides, so it cannot be verified or used to certify real improvements; its practical value is mostly rhetorical motivation for the loss function design rather than an actionable or tight guarantee of improved sample quality.

The empirical results are not uniformly supportive of the paper's own abstract claims of 'consistent' improvement: in Table 2, QICE for TimeDiff and SSSD and CRPS/Conditional FID for TMDM/NSDiff sometimes worsen under CW, and the paper's self-reported win-rates (e.g., 79-92%) implicitly acknowledge a non-trivial fraction of cases where CW-Gen does not help, undermining the 'consistently enhances' framing used throughout the abstract/intro/conclusion.

The 'win rate' metric used in Table 1 and elsewhere is not rigorously defined (it mixes comparisons across different baselines/metrics into a single aggregate number) and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests accounting for the 10-seed repetitions) is reported, despite means and standard deviations being available, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are meaningful or within noise (e.g., TMDM CRPS 0.472 vs 0.469, clearly overlapping in variance).

Only Table 2 (ETTh1) is shown in the excerpt reviewed; if the remaining four main-result tables (Tables 3–6, referenced but not included) follow a similarly mixed pattern, the claim of consistent improvement across datasets becomes even less convincing without seeing the full picture directly in the main text rather than deferred appendices.

No direct empirical comparison to TsFlow (which also uses mean/covariance-like priors via Gaussian Processes) or GP-based baselines is provided, despite extensive discussion of TsFlow's limitations in the related work; this omission weakens the positioning claim that CW-Gen is superior to existing prior-informed approaches.

Computational cost of CW-Diff involves O(d^3 Tf) eigendecompositions per sample/step, which could be substantial for higher-dimensional datasets like Solar Energy (d=137); no wall-clock timing or scalability analysis is reported to substantiate practical feasibility relative to baseline diffusion/flow models.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) and the loss function design are both centered on the terminal distribution/initial estimator accuracy, but there is limited analysis of how estimation error in JMCE propagates through the full generative sampling trajectory (i.e., no end-to-end error bound connecting estimator accuracy to final sample quality), leaving a gap between the theoretical motivation and the complete generative pipeline actually used in practice.

strengths: The paper provides a theoretical motivation (Theorem 1) for replacing the standard terminal distribution in diffusion models with a conditionally whitened one, giving the method a principled basis rather than being purely heuristic.

CW-Gen is presented as a unifying framework: several prior approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) are shown to be special cases, which clarifies the landscape of prior-informed diffusion/flow models for time series.

The JMCE module is a reasonably well-designed joint mean-covariance estimator, using a Cholesky-based parameterization to guarantee PSD covariance and an eigenvalue regularization term to maintain numerical stability.

The framework is extended beyond diffusion to flow matching (CW-Flow), demonstrating generality, and the authors discuss computational trade-offs (eigen-decomposition cost in CW-Diff vs. avoiding inversion in CW-Flow).

Broad empirical evaluation: 6 base generative models, 5 real-world datasets of varying dimensionality/frequency, and multiple metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID, plus ProbMSE/ProbMAE in appendix), with results averaged over 10 seeds and standard deviations reported.
Qualitative illustrations (Figure 2) provide intuitive support for the claim that incorporating priors mitigates mean-shift issues from distribution shift.
weaknesses: The improvements are not fully consistent: in Table 2, several cases show CW variants performing worse on certain metrics (e.g., TimeDiff's QICE increases from 9.513 to 12.610, NsDiff's CRPS increases from 0.407 to 0.416, TMDM shows negligible or mixed changes), which somewhat undercuts the claim of 'consistent' improvement emphasized in the abstract and results section.

Theorem 1's sufficient condition depends on unknown quantities (true mean/covariance estimation errors) and the true conditional mean's norm, making it largely a qualitative/motivational result rather than an actionable or empirically verifiable guarantee; the paper does not clearly validate whether condition (3) actually holds in the real datasets used.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) is developed specifically for the diffusion/SDE setting; its extension to justify CW-Flow (flow matching) is not formally established, so the flow-matching instantiation appears comparatively more heuristic/less theoretically grounded than claimed.

Key experimental details (hyperparameter sensitivity for sliding-window size, λmin, wEigen) are fixed with limited justification or sensitivity analysis in the main text, and most dataset-level result tables (beyond ETTh1) are deferred to the appendix, making it harder to assess the full robustness of results from the main paper alone.

The paper discusses TsFlow and S2DBM as relevant related works but does not include them as empirical baselines, leaving a gap in comparison against other prior-informed generative forecasting methods.

The two-stage pipeline (pretraining JMCE, then training the whitened generative model) adds architectural and training complexity/overhead that is not clearly quantified relative to baseline single-stage training, and no wall-clock/training cost comparison is provided despite claims about efficiency differences between CW-Diff and CW-Flow.

The distribution-shift mitigation claim is primarily supported through qualitative visualization (Figure 2) rather than a dedicated quantitative experiment directly measuring distribution shift robustness (e.g., performance across train/test splits with known shift).

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical foundation (Theorem 1 and 2) establishing sufficient conditions under which replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution of diffusion models with a conditionally whitened one improves KL divergence to the true conditional distribution, with rigorous, self-contained proofs.

Unifies existing prior-informed diffusion approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases of the proposed CW-Gen framework, and clearly articulates their specific limitations (e.g., ignoring covariance, complicated reverse process) that CW-Gen addresses.

Proposes a well-motivated Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) using Cholesky parameterization and an explicit eigenvalue regularization term directly derived from the theoretical sufficient condition, which is a nice link between theory and method design.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 6 generative backbones (5 diffusion models + 1 flow matching) and 5 real-world datasets of varying dimensionality/domain, using multiple complementary metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID, ProbMSE/MAE), showing fairly consistent improvements.

Thorough ablation studies (hyperparameters wEigen/λmin, backbone choice, sliding window length, joint vs separate mean/covariance training, individual prior components) that support the design choices and increase confidence in the empirical claims.

Addresses practical computational concerns via an accelerated whitening scheme (avoiding eigen-decomposition) and an end-to-end training variant, along with reported wall-clock training times across datasets.
Includes comparisons against additional non-diffusion/flow prior-informed baselines (DSPD, TsFlow) to contextualize the contribution relative to broader literature.
weaknesses: The theoretical sufficient conditions (Theorem 1, Eq. 3; Theorem 2, Eq. 9) are never empirically verified to actually hold in the experiments; the paper only shows JMCE achieves low estimation error, not that the conditions are satisfied in practice, leaving a gap between theory and demonstrated applicability.

Method incurs cubic computational complexity O(d^3) from eigen-decomposition for CW-Diff, which becomes a serious bottleneck on higher-dimensional datasets (e.g., Solar Energy training time balloons to ~24,000s for JMCE alone), and the benefits of CW-Gen are visibly weaker on this dataset (lower win rates, mixed ProbMSE results at 50%).
Reproducibility statement provides a code link placeholder that is blank/missing, undermining the reproducibility claim despite detailed algorithmic pseudocode in the appendix.

Some individual results are inconsistent or unfavorable for CW-Gen (e.g., SSSD on Weather has worse CRPS under CW; ILI QICE win rate is only 33%), and the paper does not perform statistical significance testing across seeds despite reporting standard deviations.

The empirical comparison is restricted almost entirely to diffusion/flow-matching baselines; other established probabilistic forecasting approaches (e.g., normalizing flows, GP-copula models, deep AR-based probabilistic methods) are not compared, limiting the demonstrated positioning relative to the broader probabilistic forecasting literature.

Sensitivity to the sliding-window covariance size appears non-trivial on smaller datasets (ILI), suggesting the method's practical robustness may be dataset-dependent and require careful tuning that isn't fully characterized.

The paper is notation-heavy and dense, with many interacting components (JMCE loss terms, Cholesky whitening operations, multiple hyperparameters), which may hinder accessibility and independent reimplementation despite the provided algorithms.

strengths: The paper provides a theoretical treatment (Theorem 1, 2 with full proofs) of when modifying the terminal distribution of diffusion models with a conditional mean/covariance prior reduces the KL divergence to the true conditional distribution, offering some principled motivation for the design.

The proposed JMCE learns a full (not just diagonal) sliding-window covariance via a Cholesky-style parameterization, which is a genuine extension over prior mean/variance-only regressors like TMDM and NsDiff, and is accompanied by an eigenvalue-control regularizer to keep the estimator well-conditioned.
The framework is instantiated for both diffusion (CW-Diff) and flow matching (CW-Flow), demonstrating some generality, and is shown to be composable with six different generative backbones.

Very extensive empirical effort: five datasets, six base models, multiple metrics, many ablations (hyperparameters, backbones, sliding-window length, individual prior components, end-to-end training variant, computational cost analysis), which shows diligence in evaluation scope.
Reasonable reproducibility materials: detailed algorithms in the appendix, hyperparameter settings, and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The claimed 'consistent' improvement is overstated: for the strongest and most relevant baselines (NsDiff, TMDM — themselves prior-informed methods), CW-Gen frequently fails to improve or even hurts performance on key metrics (e.g., Table 2 NsDiff CRPS 0.407→0.431, Table 3 NsDiff CRPS/ProbCorr get worse, Table 5 SSSD CRPS gets worse under CW). The headline 'win rate' statistics aggregate across weak and strong baselines and across loosely related metrics, obscuring the fact that gains are concentrated in already-weak baselines (TimeDiff, SSSD, Diffusion-TS, FlowTS) rather than validating the core theoretical claim against the most comparable prior-based competitors.

No statistical significance testing is reported despite claiming 10 random seeds per experiment; many reported standard deviations are large relative to the Raw-vs-CW differences, making several 'wins' questionable.

The theoretical contribution, while rigorously derived, largely amounts to standard Gaussian KL-divergence algebra (Pythagorean KL decomposition, trace/eigenvalue bounds) and provides only a sufficient (not necessary) condition whose practical verifiability during training is never empirically checked (e.g., the paper never verifies condition (3) holds on real data, only argues qualitatively in Appendix D).

Scalability is a serious concern: on the highest-dimensional dataset (Solar Energy, d=137), JMCE training and conditional whitening via eigendecomposition takes ~24,185s and ~14,460s respectively (Table 19), and this dataset also shows the lowest win rate (79.17%) and weakest/most mixed gains, suggesting the proposed whitening mechanism scales poorly and loses effectiveness exactly where inter-variable correlation modeling should matter most.

The novelty is largely incremental/engineering in nature — conditional whitening with learned mean/covariance is a natural combination of existing ideas (CARD/TMDM mean regressors, NsDiff variance regressors, Cholesky-parameterized covariance, standard whitening transforms); the conceptual leap beyond prior works is modest despite the heavy theoretical machinery surrounding it.

Comparisons to closely related multivariate-covariance or GP-prior methods (TsFlow, DSPD) are weak: these methods are applied dimension-by-dimension (univariate) rather than in their intended or a fairly-adapted multivariate setting, making the comparison somewhat unfair and inconclusive.

Several ablation results undercut the paper's own design choices without clear resolution — e.g., larger penalty weights/regularization improve eigenvalue control but the interaction with accuracy is inconsistent, and using only variance or only covariance as prior sometimes degrades performance even below the Raw baseline, raising questions about the robustness and necessity of the specific proposed combination.

The abstract/conclusion's strong, sweeping claims of 'consistent' improvement across non-stationarity, correlation capture, and distribution-shift mitigation are not fully supported by the more nuanced (and often contradictory) per-table results shown in the appendix.

strengths: Provides a clear theoretical motivation (via a KL-divergence Pythagorean decomposition) for replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution of diffusion/flow models with a conditionally whitened one, with explicit sufficient conditions (Theorem 1) and comparisons against prior mean/variance-based approaches such as CARD, TMDM, and NsDiff (Theorem 2).

Proposes a principled Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) using a Cholesky-based parameterization that guarantees PSD covariance estimates and includes an eigenvalue regularizer directly motivated by the theory, rather than an ad hoc design.

The CW-Gen framework is shown to generalize/unify several existing prior-informed diffusion methods (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases, and is compatible with both diffusion (CW-Diff) and flow matching (CW-Flow) backbones.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 5 real datasets x 6 base generative models x multiple metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID, ProbMSE/MAE), plus substantial ablations on JMCE hyperparameters, backbone choice, sliding-window length, individual prior components (mean/var/cov), and comparisons to univariate prior baselines (DSPD, TsFlow).

Addresses practical concerns such as computational cost (offering a triangular-inverse alternative to eigendecomposition and an end-to-end training variant) and discusses failure regimes of the theoretical condition.
Reasonably reproducible: detailed algorithms, proofs, and implementation details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Despite the claim of 'consistent' improvement, several tables show mixed or marginal results (e.g., SSSD on Weather/Solar Energy, TMDM/NsDiff on ETTh2, QICE win-rate only 33% on ILI), and many improvements fall within overlapping standard deviations, with no statistical significance testing performed across the 10 repeated runs.

The sufficient condition in Theorem 1/2 depends on unknown quantities (true mean/covariance estimation errors, minimal eigenvalues) and is not directly verifiable in practice; its main role is as qualitative motivation rather than an actionable guarantee, somewhat limiting the practical value of the 'theory-guided' design claim.

Scalability is a real concern: on the highest-dimensional dataset (Solar Energy, d=137), JMCE training and CW whitening incur very large computational overhead (eigendecomposition cost reported as tens of thousands of seconds), and the point-forecast win rate there drops to 50%, suggesting the benefits diminish as dimensionality grows.

Baselines are restricted to diffusion/flow-matching models; no comparison is made to strong non-generative or classical probabilistic baselines (e.g., DeepAR, GP-based or normalizing-flow forecasters beyond TsFlow, or simple IRevIN-style instance normalization baselines) that could isolate how much gain comes from whitening versus just better mean/variance conditioning.

The core idea (incorporating conditional mean/covariance into the terminal distribution rather than only modulating the forward trajectory as CARD/TMDM/NsDiff do) is a meaningful but somewhat incremental extension of this existing line of work, mainly swapping diagonal variance for full covariance and simplifying the parameterization.

The sheer number of tables and ablations, while thorough, makes it harder to assess the net robustness of the central claims, and some presented 'win rate' summaries aggregate across metrics where individual gains are small or inconsistent.
